author: Talha Javaid Malik
text:
Your App is slow. Before you throw money at it, ask this one question.

Every performance problem falls into one of two buckets:

🔴 CPU-bound — the system is thinking. Crunching numbers, processing images, running ML inference, compressing files. The processor is maxed out and there's nothing else waiting around.

🔵 I/O-bound — the system is waiting. For a database, an API, a file on disk, a third-party service. The CPU is idle 90% of the time, just twiddling its thumbs.

Here's why this matters if you're the one signing off on infra spend:

Wrong diagnosis = wasted budget. If your app is I/O-bound and your engineer says "let's upgrade to a bigger server," you just paid more for a faster processor that was never the bottleneck. It's like buying a faster chef when the real problem is the waiter taking orders one table at a time.

The fixes are completely different. 
→ CPU-bound problems get solved with more compute, parallelization, or better algorithms. 
→ I/O-bound problems get solved with caching, async processing, connection pooling, or just... not waiting on things sequentially.

Throw the wrong fix at the wrong problem and you'll 3Xxx your cloud bill without moving the needle on speed.

This is also a hiring signal. When you're evaluating technical hires or vendors, ask them: "Is this bottleneck CPU-bound or I/O-bound, and how do you know?" If they can't answer clearly, they're guessing — and you're paying for the guess.
The best engineering teams I've worked with diagnose before they scale. Cheaper, faster, and it actually works.

If your product is "kind of slow" and nobody can tell you why in one sentence that's the first thing worth fixing.

🚗🔬We're hiring a postdoc or research engineer in Scientific Machine Learning for dynamical systems.

After working on lateral vehicle dynamics with Fabien Lionti, we're opening a new front: longitudinal dynamics, as part of a partnership between INRIA ACENTAURI Inria and DGA - Direction générale de l'armement focused on modernizing the numerical methods used for military vehicle testing.

🎯Ground vehicle testing today generates massive volumes of data (inertial units, onboard sensors, dedicated measurement chains). This data is rich but noisy, incomplete, and hard to fully exploit with classical physical models or purely statistical learning approaches alone.
This project sits at the intersection of two scientific directions: Physics-Informed AI, applied to the analysis and simulation of longitudinal vehicle dynamics.

🔍Possible research directions:
- Exploitation and qualification of test data (signal synchronization, drift/outlier detection, identification of dynamic regimes)
- Hybrid physics-learning modeling (stability, physical constraint compliance, interpretability), with priority given to longitudinal dynamics
- Virtual sensors and uncertainty quantification (Bayesian methods, model ensembles, GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo)

🛠️Resources:
- Computing resources dedicated to machine learning and numerical simulation
- Professional licenses (OpenAI Codex, Claude Code) to speed up prototyping and documentation
- Supervision by researchers from INRIA ACENTAURI (Sophia-Antipolis) Philippe Martinet and LERIA (Université d'Angers) Nicolas GUTOWSKI, PhD in AI, control, and robotics, alongside the DGA Techniques Terrestres teams

👤Profile:
- PhD in AI, control/automation, robotics, computational mechanics, applied mathematics, signal processing, or scientific simulation
- Strong skills in at least two of the following: ML/AI, dynamical modeling, scientific computing (Python/PyTorch/NumPy), multibody mechanics
- Experience with Physics-Informed AI, system identification, state estimation, or uncertainty quantification is a strong plus
Automotive dynamics experience is a bonus, not a requirement

📩Application: CV, cover letter, list of publications, two references, and if possible a link to code or previous work.

author: Kevin Clifford
text:
Recently I picked up a role with a SportsTech that had every unicorn-wishlist symptom I usually warn people about.

Senior AI hire. Production ML, sports domain expertise, stakeholder-facing, board-ready. Salary: mid-market, not senior-market.

Instead of running the search as written, I went back to the hiring manager with the same questions I ask everyone now: 

What actually matters in year one? 
What can this person grow into.

We cut the brief down to two non-negotiables:

- Strong production ML background,
- The ability to explain technical work to non-technical stakeholders. 
- Sports domain experience became a "nice to have, teachable in 90 days," not a gate.

That one change opened the pool from "unicorns who don't exist" to "strong engineers willing to learn sport."

Filled in five weeks. The hire's now three months in and already making an impact.

The lesson isn't "lower your standards." 

It's separate what's actually needed on day one from what can be built over the first year. 

That distinction is the difference between a role that sits open for six months and one that gets filled in less than five weeks.

author: Ada Offonry
text:
After twenty years of hiring quants and engineers for hedge funds and investment banks, I've come to realise that although job titles are useful, they do not tell the full story of your scope, skills and impact.

The same work carries different labels at different firms. For example, a platform engineer at one fund is an infrastructure engineer at the next and a production engineer at the one after that, even though the responsibilities barely change.

Some ML hires did not have ML in their title before getting those roles. They were backend engineers shipping inference pipelines or infrastructure engineers running GPU clusters.

So before you discount a job because of the title, read the job description properly:

 ➡️ What does this person own day to day
 ➡️ Which systems and tools are named
 ➡️ What has to be true for them to succeed in the first year

Then match your experience against that.

If the responsibilities look familiar, chances are you are qualified enough to apply.
